ClinicalDocument.title: SYNTHETIC RECORD, NOT A REAL MEDICAL RECORD — Pulmonology Consultation — Alexander the Great

code.originalText: Two-week review, seen the same day by pulmonology and by the clinic's addiction medicine clinician: CT of the chest, lung volumes, gas transfer and six-minute walk; chest wall pain plan; DSM-5-TR assessment and a drinking goal

text.paragraph: Left chest wall pain and breathlessness on exertion in a 32-year-old commander, years after a penetrating arrow wound of the left chest, with a reduced FVC (78 percent predicted) and a normal FEV1/FVC ratio, pleural thickening and an old rib fracture on the chest X-ray, and heavy episodic drinking. Please assess the chest, advise whether anything needs removal or surgery, and advise on pain treatment and exercise. [S]

list.item: Do the breathlessness and the low FVC come from the old wound (pleural thickening, a fibrothorax or a trapped lung), and should lung volumes and gas transfer be measured?
Is there a retained fragment, a bronchopleural fistula or loculated fluid, and does he need CT?
Does he need surgery, such as decortication or removal of a fragment?
How should the chest wall pain be treated without opioids or sedating medicines while he drinks heavily?
What exercise and breathing program do you advise, is he fit for long marches with heavy kit, and what lung function follow-up?

text.paragraph: Thank you for asking me to see Alexander, a 32-year-old army commander, for chest wall pain and breathlessness years after a penetrating arrow wound of the left chest. The history is as in your letter. The pain is localized to the scar and the rib below it, is sharp on deep breaths and twisting, and wakes him when he lies on his left side; it has never been pressing or brought on by effort alone. The breathlessness comes on at the top of long climbs and with heavy kit and settles within minutes. He has had no cough, sputum, blood, fevers, night sweats, wheeze or chest infections since the wound. He has never smoked and has no workplace dust exposure. He drank less at two banquets this fortnight and saw the addiction medicine clinician this morning. [S]
Historical basis. These claims are historical evidence, not findings from a modern examination.

list.item: Plutarch, writing about four centuries later, says he was born early in the month Hecatombaeon (the Macedonian Lous), on the sixth day, the day the temple of Artemis at Ephesus burned; the Loeb editor dates this to 356 BC and notes that the month corresponds nearly to July, and that the date may have been moved to fit the coincidence. He was born at Pella in Macedonia, the son of King Philip II and Olympias of Epirus. [D]

Ancient historians record many battle wounds: a sword wound to the thigh at Issus, a catapult bolt through shield and breastplate into the shoulder at Gaza, from which he 'was not easily cured', and a blow to the head at the Granicus. In a speech that Arrian writes for him, he says that no part of the front of his body is free from wounds. [D]

Storming a town of the Malli in the Indus valley (326 or 325 BC), he was shot with an arrow under the breast through his breastplate into the chest; Arrian cites Ptolemy that air was breathed out from the wound with the blood. He fainted from loss of blood, the arrowhead lodged at a rib was cut out, he swooned again at its removal, and Plutarch says it brought him to death's door, but he recovered after a long time under regimen and treatment. [D]

Physicians writing since have read the Malli wound as a tension pneumothorax with injury to the upper lobe of the left lung; others have argued that his recovery and return to the saddle within days make a pneumothorax unlikely. How he recovered is scarcely recorded. [R]

In Cilicia in 333 BC he fell gravely ill, according to Aristobulus from his toils, and according to other writers after bathing in the cold river Cydnus, with convulsions, high fever and sleeplessness; his physician, Philip the Acarnanian, treated him and he recovered. [D]

The ancient historians describe long drinking parties with his Companions, especially in his later years, and disagreed about how much he drank: Aristobulus, quoted by Arrian, held that he 'was not a great wine-drinker' and sat long over wine for companionship, and Plutarch that he was 'less addicted to wine than was generally believed'; Plutarch also tells of a contest in drinking unmixed wine after which the winner and many others died. [D]
During a drinking party in Sogdiana (328 BC) he killed his officer Clitus. [D]

In October 324 BC at Ecbatana, during games and drinking parties, his closest companion Hephaestion fell sick with a fever and died on about the seventh day. The historians agree that his grief was great: until the third day he neither ate nor cared for his appearance, and the mourning lasted many days. Accounts that he hanged or crucified the physician differ. [D]
After the mourning he campaigned against the Cossaeans in the mountains in winter, and in the spring of 323 BC marched back to Babylon, meeting embassies on the road. [D]

S — Synthetic modern diagnosis made at the consultation, anchored to the documented arrow wound; not a claim about his real chest.

S — Synthetic modern finding of the CT and lung function tests at the consultation, anchored to the documented arrow wound; the retrospective pneumothorax (CLM-0004) is not used.

Alcohol use disorder, mild (three DSM-5-TR criteria): drinking more than intended at banquets, riding after drinking, and arguments with his officers while drunk; ten or more drinks on two or three nights a week, more since his bereavement; no withdrawal; AUDIT 19; PEth 236 ng/mL

S — Synthetic modern diagnosis made with the addiction medicine clinician at the consultation visit, anchored to the documented drinking parties; the criteria, amounts and scores are synthetic. The diagnosis is mild, in keeping with the disputed evidence (CLM-0008).

Bereavement five months after the death of his closest companion since boyhood, with depressive symptoms (PHQ-9 12, item 9 scored 0) that do not meet criteria for a major depressive episode; prolonged grief disorder cannot be diagnosed before twelve months
S — Synthetic modern assessment anchored to the documented bereavement; DSM-5-TR codes uncomplicated bereavement as Z63.4 whatever the relationship. Not a claim about his real mental health.

list.item: Chronic post-traumatic chest wall pain (G89.21). Intercostal neuropathic pain at the healed wound and rib fracture, with allodynia over the scar. The pain is not pleuritic in the sense of active pleural disease, and nothing suggests a cardiac cause. [S]

Localized left fibrothorax after an old hemothorax (J94.1). Organized pleural thickening from an old hemothorax, with a mild restrictive defect from outside the lung and normal gas transfer; the lung beneath is expanded and there is no trapped lung, retained fragment or fistula. Part of the low FVC is splinting from pain. His exercise capacity is normal for his age. [S]
Fitness for heavy exertion. No limit from the lungs on marches or heavy kit; breathlessness at the top of long climbs is expected to improve with training and less pain. [S]

text.paragraph: Data reviewed: Chest X-ray and spirometry from intake (FVC 3.92 L, 78 percent; FEV1 3.29 L, 79 percent; ratio 0.84). Today's CT of the chest without contrast: localized pleural thickening up to 7 mm over the left lateral and posterior lower chest with a thin rim of calcification, consistent with an old organized hemothorax; a linear subpleural scar along the wound track in the left lower lobe with slight volume loss; a healed fifth rib fracture with callus; no retained metallic or other foreign body, no fistula, loculated fluid, empyema, nodule or emphysema. Today's lung volumes: TLC 5.28 L, 79 percent predicted, a mild restrictive defect; DLCO 31.4 mL/min/mmHg (about 94 percent predicted) with a high KCO, the pattern of restriction from outside the lung. Six-minute walk: 548 m, saturation 98 to 96 percent, Borg 3, chest pain 5 of 10 at the end. Liver tests from intake. [S]

list.item: Lung volumes and gas transfer today confirm mild extraparenchymal restriction with normal DLCO; no further tests are needed now (question 1). [S]
CT shows no retained fragment, fistula or loculated fluid; no further imaging unless symptoms change (question 2). [S]
No surgery: decortication is kept for a trapped lung or severe restriction, and a localized fibrothorax with a TLC of 79 percent is neither (question 3). [S]

Lidocaine 5% patch over the scar for up to 12 hours a day, with acetaminophen within 2,000 mg a day; avoid opioids, tramadol, gabapentinoids and benzodiazepines while he drinks heavily; a telephone check in four weeks; an intercostal nerve block if pain stays above 4 of 10 after six weeks (question 4). [S]
Physical therapy for thoracic mobility and scar desensitization, deep-breathing exercises and graded aerobic and strength training back to long marches; he may continue full duty (question 5). [S]
Repeat spirometry in about two months; then yearly, or sooner if breathlessness returns (question 5). [S]
Return sooner for fever, cough with sputum or blood, new pleuritic pain or worsening breathlessness. [S]

Discussed with the patient, who agreed with the plan, and with Dr. Papadakis-Mensah the same day; the clinic's addiction medicine clinician, who saw him this morning, will lead the drinking plan, and I have avoided any pain medicine that would interfere with it. [S]
Follow-up: Pulmonology review in a year with spirometry, or sooner if needed; repeat spirometry in primary care in about two months. [S]
